procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad (Iqbal Ahmad C. J. and Allsop J.) dated 31st August, 1944, in a reference under section 66 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Income-tax Tribunal referred two questions to the High Court under section 66 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. The High Court answered those questions, and this order was appealed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The New Piecegoods Bazar Co. Ltd. appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and answered the two questions referred by the Income-tax Tribunal in the affirmative.

directions: The two questions which were referred to the High Court by the Income-tax Tribunal and cited above are answered in the affirmative.
The appellants will have their costs in the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the amount of house-tax and the amount of water-tax, imposed by the Municipal Board of Allahabad under section 128, sub-section (l) clauses (i) and (x), respectively of the United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916, and paid by the owner as a lessor under section 149 of that Act should be deducted as an allowance from the bona fide annual value of the property on the ground that such amount is an annual charge, which is not a capital charge to which the property is subject within the meaning of clause (iv) of sub-section (1) of section 9 of the Indian Income-tax Act.

facts: The case involved house-tax and water-tax imposed by the Municipal Board of Allahabad under the United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916.
The taxes were paid by the property owner, who was also the lessor (landlord).
The owner sought to deduct these tax payments from the property's 'bona fide annual value' for income tax purposes.
law: Section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, allows for a deduction for an 'annual charge not being a capital charge to which the property is subject'.
Section 177 of the United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916, states that taxes imposed on the annual value of buildings or lands shall 'be a first charge upon such buildings or lands'.
The Court relied on the precedent set in a similar case, *New Piecegoods Bazar Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay*.
application: The Supreme Court's decision was primarily based on applying the reasoning from the precedent case, *New Piecegoods Bazar Co. Ltd.*
The Court compared the relevant law in this case (the United Provinces Municipalities Act) with the law in the precedent case (the Bombay Act) and found them to be 'substantially similar'.
Specifically, the Court noted that Section 177 of the United Provinces Act makes the municipal taxes a 'first charge' on the property itself.

Because the tax is a legal charge on the property, it directly fits the definition of an 'annual charge... to which the property is subject' as required by Section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the municipal taxes were a statutory 'charge' on the property under the U.P. Municipalities Act, they qualified for the deduction allowed under Section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act. Therefore, the amount paid for house-tax and water-tax could be deducted from the property's annual value for income tax calculation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the amount of house-tax and the amount of water-tax, imposed by the Municipal Board of Allahabad under section 128, sub-section (l) clauses (i) and (x), respectively of the United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916, and paid by the owner as a lessor under section 149 of that Act should be deducted as an allowance from the bona fide annual value of the property on the ground that such amount is an annual charge, which is not a capital charge to which the property is subject within the meaning of clause (iv) of sub-section (1) of section 9 of the Indian Income-tax Act.
appellant_arguments: The house-tax and water-tax paid by the owner under the United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916, qualify as an 'annual charge, which is not a capital charge' to which the property is subject, within the meaning of section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act. Therefore, these amounts should be deducted from the property's annual value when calculating income tax.
respondent_arguments: The house-tax and water-tax paid by the owner do not constitute an 'annual charge' as contemplated by section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act and, consequently, should not be deducted from the property's annual value.

cases.case_name: New Piecegoods Bazar Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay
cases.principle: The court relied on the reasoning and decision in this case, which dealt with substantially similar provisions of the Bombay Act, to determine the deductibility of municipal taxes from the annual value of a property for income tax purposes.

cases.case_name: Gappumal Kanhaiya Lal v. Commissioner of Income-tax
cases.principle: The court approved the reasoning in this connected appeal, stating it took the correct view on the matter of deducting municipal house and water taxes from the annual value of a property.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: House-tax and water-tax imposed by a municipality under the United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916, and paid by the owner as a lessor, are considered "annual charges not being capital charges to which the property is subject" within the meaning of Section 9(1)(iv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. Consequently, these amounts are deductible from the property's bona fide annual value for income tax purposes.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the house-tax and water-tax imposed under the United Provinces Municipalities Act, 1916, are deductible from the annual value of a property for income tax purposes. This decision was reached not by independent analysis, but by incorporating the reasoning of a prior decision, *New Piecegoods Bazar Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay*. The court found that the provisions of the United Provinces Act regarding the levy of these taxes were "substantially similar" to the provisions of the Bombay Act discussed in that precedent, and therefore, the same legal conclusion must apply.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied a comparative analysis to determine if the statutory provisions of the United Provinces Act were "substantially similar" to the provisions of the Bombay Act, which had been interpreted in a binding precedent.

The court applied the doctrine of stare decisis, holding that the reasoning and outcome of a prior, factually similar case (*New Piecegoods Bazar Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay*) were controlling.
